results.title: First Hand: five films
results.brief_description:
First Hand is a Koorie Heritage Trust cultural training and media project for young Indigenous people in Melbourne and regional areas. The project gives young Koories the skills to explore questions of culture and identity through the moving image.
During late 2004 and early 2005, participants completed training in communications, media and cultural studies, practical workshops in video production and a scriptwriting workshop held in the Screen Pit at ACMI. Community elders from metropolitan and regional areas (including Uncle Wally Cooper, Aunty Joy Wandin-Murphy and Uncle Sandy Atkinson) facilitated discussions about Indigenous culture and identity.

results.title: No dedication (no education)
results.brief_description: This film is part documentary and part music video. On Sunday 17th April 2005, Johnny Mac, a Koorie MC from Melbourne, performed at an outdoor concert and BBQ for 40 odd kids and their parents at the Ballarat Aboriginal Cooperative. The theme of the song and the day was education and the kids captured footage of the show and interviewed their parents and Elders about their school days.

results.title: In this situation again = In this place again
results.brief_description:
This is a documentary film about the friendship between an inmate at Bendigo Prison, Shane Lovett, and a young Koorie called Tim from Heywood. Tim visits Shane at the prison to talk about the music he has been making and what life is like in prison.
Music: “Barganji River Tribe” Shane Lovett and Sonny Wise; “Only Dreaming” Shane Lovett; “So Go” Shane Lovett

results.title: St. Albans: an ethnic programme (TEFC)
results.creator_credit: Ian Hart and Canberra. College of Advanced Education. Media Centre
results.brief_description: St Albans is a multilingual, multicultural community where 85% of the population are migrants from non-English speaking countries. St Albans East primary school, with a schools commission grant, employ parents in a program to increase the children’s awareness of community languages and culture.

results.title: Design for climate
results.creator_credit: Nicholas Alexander, S.T. Evans and Building Research and Development Advisory Committee
results.brief_description: Research on problems of building design for Australian conditions. Maintaining an acceptable indoor climate by economic means involves a building of suitable thermal characteristics using insulation and heating and cooling as required, proper lighting and ventilation. The noise problem, protection of external surfaces and relating the building to its environment for best use of the natural climate are considered.

results.title: Memories: a short walk with Aunty Maude
results.brief_description: This is a documentary film about the childhood and life of Aunty Maude Alberts, a Gundijimara Elder and the filmmaker’s grandmother. With her children and grandchildren Aunty Maude visits “the old place”, a property outside of Heywood where she grew up. The film makes a poetic exploration of Aunty Maude’s upbringing and the passing on of her traditional knowledge to her children and grandchildren.

results.title: Old man: returning to Lake Condah Mission

video_links.name: Old man: returning to Lake Condah Mission

results.brief_description: This is a documentary film about growing up on Lake Condah Aboriginal Mission. A local Elder, Uncle Kenny Saunders, visits the site of Lake Condah Mission and talks about his childhood memories revealing a past of cruelty and fear, and the devastation felt in the aftermath of the Eumerella massacres.

results.title: The Ferals [Puppets]
results.credit_line:
Designed by Garth Frost

Puppet maker Tina Matthews

Australia, 1993

Courtesy of Emma de Vries

Edie Kurzer, Australia, 2020
results.brief_description: “They discovered fame and fortune and they’re never going back.” Or so proclaimed the catchy hook of The Ferals TV theme song. This kids’ program debuted on ABC TV in 1994 and then, after two successful seasons, it has endured in Australian pop culture. Capitalising on the grunge aesthetic of the time, it followed an unruly bunch of feral animals living in a share house with flatmates played by human actors. The ditzy rabbit Mixy and sassy cat Modigliana were key members of the show, adding to the tradition of children’s programming featuring puppets in starring roles, including Lift Off (1992-95) and Mr Squiggle (1959-99).

constellations_other.name: Australian TV in the 1990s
constellations_other.description: In the 1990s, Australians and Australian culture was changing: so too were the representations of it on television.

results.title: CURIOUS
results.brief_description: Edie Kurzer approached curating CURIOUS much like she does when designing costume for film and TV – by taking inspiration from found objects and combining them to exceed their original function, while also avoiding the obvious.

constellations_primary.name: Clothing, country, character
constellations_primary.description: Edie Kurzer's costume design work on Judy & Punch and Picnic at Hanging Rock is part of a larger trend in Australian films and TV series.

results.description:
When Edie Kurzer is designing costumes for film and TV, she often takes inspiration from found objects. It’s a similar approach to how she has curated these cabinets of curios and memorabilia. Like the details of a costume, when presented together as a collection these objects become more than the sum of their parts. According to Kurzer, “each of the objects have a story to tell, brought together by the common denominator of the moving image”.

Within the cabinets, examples such as the Pez collection or the character figurines celebrate familiar film and TV characters that have escaped the frame and live on as part of our collective memory. Kurzer also acknowledges the behind-the-scenes roles of various creative departments in film and television production through the display of everyday items that are commonly used – a paintbrush, a pair of scissors or a handy wire coat hanger.

In collecting, creating and curating these objects for display, Kurzer adheres to her rule of avoiding the obvious and celebrating the unexpected.

You can see examples of Edie Kurzer’s costume work in The Story of the Moving Image.
